A user makes the following post on a social media site:

What projects are keeping you busy?
Hey everyone! 👋 I’m always curious about what people are working on - whether it’s a creative side hustle, a startup idea, or just something fun. What’s keeping you busy these days? Share your project below, and let’s connect! Maybe we can trade tips or ideas. 🙌 Can’t wait to see what you’re up to! ✌️



They receive the following reply to their post:

Oh hey! So, I’ve been diving into a couple of things. I’ve just started a small herb garden on my balcony, which is a big deal for me because I’m *not* known for keeping plants alive, like at all. It’s been surprisingly calming every morning to check on them and see if I somehow managed to not kill them. Also, I’ve been trying to write a little cookbook for my kids with all my family's recipes. I always wanted them to have a piece of our traditions in a fun way. And then there’s this online pottery class I signed up for. I’m basically just playing with clay like a little kid, but hey, I made a lopsided mug the other day, and I’m oddly proud of it. What about you? You got any fun projects or maybe something that’s been nudging at your curiosity lately?

Or at least be fully transparent on ad tier audience reach and adjust prices accordingly when there ad tier audience drops. I probably know nothing.



They receive the following reply to their post:

Man, this is total garbage. Imagine paying for ads and then having platforms practically blackmail people into paying more to avoid those ads. It's like they're double-dipping and we're just supposed to be cool with it? Nah, I don't buy that. They should be upfront about how many people are actually seeing our ads and charge us based on that real number. Otherwise, it's like they’re running a scam. It's definitely something that needs more attention because advertisers are getting played if you ask me.

A user makes the following post on a social media site:

What is your favorite font right now?
Hello, community! Since there are a lot of designers here, I'm curious to know what typeface you can live without right now and that has you a little bit obsessed. I think it can help us inspire each other. Until a few years ago I was completely obsessed with Monument Extended or Gotham style fonts. I made a lot of Drum&Bass style electronic music posters and that aggressive and forceful character definitely worked very well with my clients. However, I feel that from now on many designs have been oversaturated with this font and I hate it. I am currently fully into Europa Grotesk in all its forms. I love its simplicity. I look forward to reading you!



They receive the following reply to their post:

Oh man, Monument Extended had its moment, didn't it? It was like the go-to for anything that needed to scream "Look at me!" It's funny how we can get so attached to certain fonts only to end up wanting to run away from them. For me, I’ve been pretty fixated on GT America lately. There’s something about its versatility that really does it for me, especially when you’re juggling between modern and classic design vibes. I used it recently for a friend's startup branding, and it just gave the entire project this sleek and timeless feel. But I get the whole Europa Grotesk thing—I used it for a minimalistic project a while back and it just had that perfect balance of clean and personable. It's got a kinda neutrality about it that makes it super adaptable. Fonts can be like music styles; sometimes you just need a change of taste to keep the inspiration flowing. Anyway, I’m sure my font obsession will switch up again soon. It's like every time I see a new typeface I get a little crush and just have to start using it everywhere.

A user makes the following post on a social media site:

$50 but everyone gets a splinter
You get, legally, untraceably, and untaxably, $50 dollars in your bank account or in cash (your choice) BUT everyone in the world gets a small splinter of wood instantly imbedded between their index and middle finger on their dominant hand. It's an ordinary splinter, that acts like an average everyday splinter, and can be removed with the usual methods.



They receive the following reply to their post:

So, I’m thinking it sounds like a harmless deal at first, right? I mean, 50 bucks is 50 bucks, and who doesn’t want a little extra cash for basically nothing? But then, when you really think about it, everyone, and I mean everyone, getting a splinter might cause a bit of chaos. Imagine surgeons, right in the middle of something important, teachers writing on whiteboards, or just regular folks trying to go about their day. I guess getting everyone a minor inconvenience might not be worth a quick $50. Plus, have you ever had a splinter in such a sensitive spot? That stuff can be annoying and painful. And then, there’s the sheer number of people affected. Like, what if someone’s doing something really important and that little splinter makes them mess up? Weird to think about it on such a big scale. I’m probably just overthinking it, but it makes you wonder about those tiny annoyances and how they add up.

A user makes the following post on a social media site:

DAE get the urge to "flex" their muscles?
For as long as I can remember, I've always had this urge to flex my upper body?? I'll try to describe it as best I can; I can be doing anything when I get this strong feeling to pull my clenched/clasped fists into my chest and flex my muscles. It's mostly my arm/chest/back muscles, but sometimes my legs and feet join in too. I wouldn't describe the urge as an itch or a tingle, it's almost like my brain is just telling my body to do it, kind of like breathing. Does anyone else experience this? I've never talked about this with anybody, mainly because I wasn't sure how to describe it. I've been doing it for so long, it's like trying to describe my heart beating.



They receive the following reply to their post:

I've definitely had moments where I feel this weird compulsion to flex, especially when I was working out regularly. It’s like my muscles are reminding me they're there or something. It’s kind of funny, because it’s like giving yourself a mini workout without even meaning to. When I was younger, I used flexing like a stress reliever, I guess. Like if I was anxious, I'd flex, and somehow it felt like I was grounding myself. Maybe it’s just some primal instinct thing? In any case, it seems pretty normal to me. I wouldn’t worry too much unless it's hurting or something. But yeah, I’d say that’s part of the human experience, just those quirky things we do without really knowing why. We all have our quirks, right?

A user makes the following post on a social media site:

A 3-4 Week Budget Backpacking Itinerary in Europe (Starting from Paris, Safe for Solo Travelers?)
Hey everyone, I’m planning a 3 to 4-week solo backpacking trip across Europe this August, starting from Paris. My goal is to keep costs low, explore multiple destinations, and spend no more than 1-2 days in each place. 🎒🚆🏕️ I’d love your suggestions for: * An efficient itinerary covering main cities and beautiful must-see places across different countries. * Tips for cheap travel options (trains, buses, budget airlines). * Camping-friendly or affordable accommodations along the way. * Insights on whether these routes and destinations are safe for a solo traveler. If you’ve done solo backpacking or have any recommendations for safe and affordable routes, I’d be super grateful to hear your advice! Thanks so much for your help! 🙏 What’s your go-to route for solo backpacking in Europe on a budget? 🌍



They receive the following reply to their post:

Oh man, running around Europe in just 1-2 days per city is brutal. Like, are you really gonna "see" anything, or just collect stamps on your Instagram? There's a big difference between rushing and traveling. Chill a bit, maybe pick fewer places but spend more time in each, otherwise, you're just ticking boxes. You know trains aren't always the cheapest, right? Buses are slow and suck but can save you cash. Look at rideshares too, but keep your wits about you. Hostels are your friend; Campgrounds too, if you want to live wild for a night. Just don’t go expecting every city’s gonna be all Paris-level safety. Some hoods in big cities are sketchy after dark no matter where you are, so stay sharp. But hey, go crazy, get lost, and most importantly, have fun. Just don't expect some magical Eurotrip movie scenes at every corner.

A user makes the following post on a social media site:

I needed my startup to fail to build my first successful business
My first startup failed, but it was exactly what I needed to get to where I am today. Here's what happened: I made the classic first-time founder mistake - I built a vitamin instead of a painkiller. I spent too much time building and not nearly enough time talking to customers. **But failing taught me the most valuable lessons:** * Always validate ideas before building anything * Sell before building * Solving urgent problems people will pay for * Always, always, be talking to customers, right from day 1 One of my biggest learnings came from struggling with cold outreach. I noticed that the only customers we landed were the ones already searching for what we offered. I wasn’t convincing anyone, just finding the right people at the right time. Every day, I spent hours scouring the internet for these conversations. After talking to other founders, I realized this wasn’t just my problem - it was a universal pain point. Cold outreach is brutal, often converting at less than 1%. What founders really need isn’t just more outreach, it’s a way to reach customers the moment they’re ready to buy. That's how I came up with the idea for my new startup. I realized there’s a massive opportunity to help businesses find customers at the perfect moment by using AI to monitor online platforms. And since I started working on this, the interest I’ve been getting from customers has been insane - it’s a crazy experience to (finally!) be solving an urgent problem. So to my fellow founders: failure isn't the end, it’s just part of the process. Every lesson, every misstep, and every pivot makes you stronger. The only way you truly fail is if you stop trying. Sometimes you need to build the wrong thing first to learn how to build the right thing. Keep going! 



They receive the following reply to their post:

Whoa, big surprise—a startup failure turned into a learning experience. Listen, failing isn’t some magical stepping stone that leads to success for everyone. The reality is a lot of people just fail and that’s it, period! Sure, your story sounds great and motivational, but let’s be blunt; most people never recover or succeed after a flop. Your belief in always "talking to customers" sounds more like common sense than some groundbreaking strategy. Like, duh, ask people what they want before you create something no one asked for. The whole "building the wrong thing first" doesn’t automatically teach you the right thing to do next. You're lucky things worked out for you the second time around. For every success story like yours, there are a bunch that go down the drain. Keep that in mind before you go telling everyone it’s just a step in the journey.

Is my book going to be boring?
Just coming to the end of the rewrite of my novel. The first draft was arguably action packed, but very much plot driven. This go round the characters feel far more alive, my new rule has been to exclude any plot points that aren't driven by character. That is to say, every scene has to follow casually from a characters situation/emotional state. Not be driven by some future state (ditcated by a ploy idea) which teleologically pulls them in one direction or the other. On the surface this seems the right way forward, but I'm worried that my novel is losing many action scenes and is more dialogue heavy. Not necessarily a bad thing, but it has made me concerned - is my book going to be boring? And if so... would I even know? Are there any litmus tests for how interesting a text will be to others?

A user makes the following post on a social media site:

I want to work a traveling job and bring my kids.
In a few years I should be able to take contracts as a traveler. I will have a truck and whatever size trailer I need for us. Is it crazy to want to home school my kids and live at different State parks with them and my wife? I want my kids to be with nature, they don't use any electronics, we spend a lot of time together, and I can't think about any downsides besides them being socially weird, but I have plans for that. I don't think living together in the woods full time is any different than in the past. They will meet people, and we will venture into society often. Of course we can make play dates. Am I thinking crazy or is this doable?



They receive the following reply to their post:

I don’t think you’re crazy at all. Actually, it sounds like an amazing experience for your family. I know a family from back home who did something kinda similar. They got a camper and traveled around the country for a year or two, homeschooling their kids. Yeah, there are definitely challenges, like unhooking your trailer or sleeping in stores’ parking lots one night cuz campsites were full. But their kids loved it and got to experience so many different things and places. They even made new friends. Your kids might end up being "socially weird," but not in a bad way—more like quirky and with a lot of unique insights and experiences. Plus, homeschooling lets you be flexible with their education, tailoring it to what interests them while ensuring they hit the basics. Though, as kids get older, like into high school, it might get harder to keep them interested unless they're truly into nature and the travel lifestyle. Socialization can totally be managed with activities, sports leagues, and homeschool groups you find along the way.

A user makes the following post on a social media site:

IsItBullshit: possible scam by supposedly fundraising company.
I've been recommended several ads by this site called OneClickKindness, which is supposedly a fundraising company for shelters. Yet what seems fishy is the fact that they ask for you to copy and paste a pre-made review for a business that has absolutely nothing to do with the cause. They say you're supporting them by doing this because of the following: "Businesses participate in this trade-off because it’s a win-win. When you leave a review, it boosts their online presence, a big deal in today's internet-driven market. In exchange, they give back by donating to animal shelters. It's a smart move for them - they get the visibility they need and also get to show their customers that they're about more than just profits; they care about making a difference too." Yet still I think this makes no sense at all, the reviews are made so that comments on the businesses seem legit and boost them, while there's absolutely no proof whatsoever that this is going to help raise funds and help animals. Here's the link to their website so you can give your thoughts on it: https://oneclickkindness.com/newLP-2steps/?fbclid=PAZXh0bgNhZW0CMTEAAaa19NZZW8lu_3ny7rEAT6Xo3_PFvypJuR4z7wAqJLBp_nlpnMqKF1W0soI_aem_SIOagX-6AhgZcbGnbLniGA



They receive the following reply to their post:

I hear ya, and this does indeed sound pretty sketchy to me. I got a nose for these things after spending way too much time in the digital world, and your gut feeling is rarely wrong. First off, that whole copy-and-paste a review thing is a red flag. Reviews should be honest, and anything asking you to just copy-and-paste feels manipulative. Plus, there’s no transparency. Legitimate organizations usually go out of their way to show exactly how things work, where the money or benefits go, and who gets helped. I’ve seen how reliable fundraising sites work, and they usually have clear pathways for donations and information on partnerships. Random reviews for an unrelated business seem like a roundabout and unreliable way to fundraise. When in doubt, I always double-check a non-profit’s legitimacy by looking them up on charity evaluators or respected watchdog sites. Usually, legitimate causes have no problem passing the sniff check (i.e., by sites like Charity Navigator or GuideStar). If you’re looking to support shelters, it’s safest to donate directly to them. It’s a better guarantee for how your contribution is used. So I think you’re right to be cautious.

A user makes the following post on a social media site:

Wrote a short story , require critique and also feedback on if it has potential for further exploring the world (5724 words)
Hey guys , I wrote this story after getting inspired by a quote from batman vs superman. I need your critique on how it turned out and if it has potential for further exploration of the world. Edit - the central theme of this story is courage and defiance in the face of overwhelming power Thanks [Aragon’s defiance ](https://docs.google.com/document/d/17WEczcdweTVIkoRpYQvW9-_VwapYtu5r/edit?usp=drivesdk&ouid=106063866026625600825&rtpof=true&sd=true)



They receive the following reply to their post:

Hey! First off, props to you for taking the leap and writing this story. From what you said about the theme of courage and defiance in the face of power, it sounds like a great starting point. I've had a blast exploring worlds in stories, so I can totally see the potential here. Now, I’m no literary expert, but I’ve tinkered with my fair share of first drafts. While I haven’t yet clicked on your document, I’m already curious about Aragon—like, what drives them to stand up against the odds? It's always cool when characters have those relatable motivations and fears. If your world allows for more depth, you could explore stuff like what injustices or power systems exist? Imagining how regular folks live and resist within that world can be super inspiring. And hey, the fact that you’re considering turning it into something bigger means you might already have a bunch of ideas bubbling up. Sometimes while scribbling down story bits, I found myself layering in details without even realizing it, like food markets with funny scents or those quirky festivals, and they’re perfect for expanding later. Oh, and don’t be afraid to let your characters make mistakes or even shift alliances. When expanding a world, those twisty paths and decisions can make the narrative a lot more gripping. Just keep writing more and adding those small details—that's how you really breathe life into your world. I’m excited for you and where you might take this... keep us posted, yeah?

A user makes the following post on a social media site:

Will Magazines still ban me if I got the basic basic concept from AI but wrote the story entirely by hand?
Most magazines ban any work that is "translated, written, developed, or assisted" by ai, and to be clear I agree with this policy. Back when I did use ai, I don't anymore, I workshopped a concept with chatgpt and it gave a suggestion for the conflict of a story with this concept that I really like. Because that idea came from AI should I drop it, to be clear the actual story is being entirely written by me with one plot element suggested by Chatgpt.



They receive the following reply to their post:

Yeah, that's a tricky spot you're in. I know a lot of places are being extra cautious about AI involvement, even if it’s just a sprinkle. And I get it, that idea’s tempting. Imagine if someone told Shakespeare, “Oh no, that Hamlet idea? Too basic; it’s banned now.” So, here’s the thing, when you're creating something, your own twists and turns matter a lot. Maybe tweak that AI-sparked idea until it's got your personal touch all over it. Like, you don’t want to risk a magazine thinking, “Oh, okay, this is the same story that everyone’s going to get if they just ask a chatbot.” But honestly, you might just want to reach out to some of the magazines and ask them how they’d feel about it. Sometimes being upfront and clear can get you some insights that you didn’t expect. Who knows? They might just say, “Yeah, If it’s got a personal touch, we’re interested.” Or you could look at this the other way, maybe come up with an entirely new idea that’s just all you, but you know, these things can lead to something even more amazing in the end. I'm not sure what's next for you or AI... there's probably a space—there's a space for everything these days.

A user makes the following post on a social media site:

Posting on wattpad/similar sites to encourage writing?
So, I'm a pretty bad when it comes to motivation. Like, I will stop being motivated to write a new chapter for months. Recently I started using wattpad and I've gotten good at updating multiple times a week, just because there's that motivation *the readers are waiting* and *my rank will drop if I don't update.* I'm not even looking for feedback, or money, or popularity, I just want to write and wattpad helps me do that. That said, I'm afraid of potential troubles if I want to really publish my work one day. If I just deleted my work from wattpad, would that be fiine?



They receive the following reply to their post:

Honestly, I think you’re on a good path. When I decided to write more seriously, I did something similar for a while too. It’s amazing how having even a tiny audience can make a big difference in motivation. Like, knowing someone out there is waiting for the next chapter can really light a fire under you. As for publishing, I wouldn’t stress too much about it. If you decide to take down your work from wattpad later, it should be okay. I mean, you hold the rights to your writing, so generally you’re free to do what you want with it. Just make sure you’re clear on terms and conditions of the site. Remember to save all your drafts offline too. You wouldn't want to lose everything if something happens to the site or your account. Plus, as you keep writing and improving, you might find you want to tweak things before going the traditional publishing route anyway.
